vignette: A 27-year-old woman, three days into a chest infection, says her heart is racing. Temperature 38.4 °C. Lead II rhythm strip:
hints: Is there a P wave in front of every QRS?
Upright P before every beat, regular, about 120/min. Nothing fancy.
explanation: A regular narrow-complex rhythm at about 125/min with an upright P wave before every QRS and a constant PR interval. That is sinus rhythm, just fast. Fever, pain, dehydration, anaemia, anxiety, PE and thyrotoxicosis are the usual drivers; the real job is finding the cause.
features: Upright P wave before every QRS in lead II
pearl: Sinus tachycardia is a sign, not a diagnosis. A rate fixed at exactly 150/min should make you hunt for flutter waves instead.

vignette: A 71-year-old woman on a beta blocker and diltiazem has a routine ECG at her GP check-up. She feels fine.
hints: Measure from the start of the P wave to the start of the QRS.
Every P conducts. The PR is long, but it never changes.
explanation: Every P wave is followed by a QRS, the rhythm is regular, and the PR interval is fixed at about 290 ms. A PR over 200 ms (one big square) with no dropped beats is first-degree AV block. AV-nodal drugs, like this combination, are a classic cause; so are high vagal tone in athletes and age-related conduction disease.
features: PR constant from beat to beat
Every P wave conducts: no dropped beats
pearl: One big square is 200 ms. If the PR is longer than one big square, it is first-degree block. It is really 'AV delay', not block: nothing is actually blocked.

vignette: A 22-year-old non-binary university rower has a pre-season ECG. They feel well; resting pulse is slow and a little irregular.
hints: Look at the PR interval, beat by beat.
The PR stretches, then one P wave stands alone with no QRS.
explanation: The PR interval lengthens with each beat (about 190, 290, then 340 ms) until a P wave fails to conduct; the cycle then resets with the shortest PR. That gives grouped beating. The block is usually in the AV node, so it is often benign in athletes, during sleep and with high vagal tone, though drugs and inferior MI can cause it too.
features: Then a non-conducted P wave (dropped QRS)
Shortest PR straight after the pause; grouped beating
pearl: Compare the PR just before and just after the dropped beat. Different: Wenckebach. Identical: think Mobitz II.

vignette: A 41-year-old Filipino man fainted overnight while sleeping off a fever of 39.5 °C. His uncle died suddenly in his sleep at 45.
hints: Focus on V1 and V2. Ignore everything else.
Coved ST elevation of at least 2 mm sloping straight into an inverted T wave.
explanation: Coved ST elevation of 2 mm or more in V1–V2, sloping down into inverted T waves, with a pseudo-RBBB terminal r′ and otherwise normal leads: the type 1 Brugada pattern, the only diagnostic type. Fever, some drugs and alcohol can unmask it. It is more common in men and in people of Southeast Asian heritage. Syncope plus a family history of sudden death are high-risk features.
features: Coved ST elevation ≥2 mm in V1–V2
ST slopes down into inverted T waves
r′ in V1, no reciprocal change, other leads normal
pearl: Recording V1–V2 one or two rib spaces higher increases the chance of catching a type 1 pattern.

vignette: A 31-year-old wheelchair basketballer in the national Paralympic squad has a routine pre-season ECG. She feels great.
hints: Count the big squares between beats. What's the rate?
Is there a normal P wave before every QRS?
explanation: A regular rhythm at about 46/min with a normal P wave before every QRS and a normal PR interval: sinus bradycardia. In trained athletes it is usually physiological, from high vagal tone and a big stroke volume. Other causes include beta blockers, hypothyroidism, sleep, raised intracranial pressure and sinus node disease.
features: Normal P before every QRS; PR about 170 ms
pearl: Rate shortcut: 300 ÷ number of big squares between R waves. About six and a half big squares here, so roughly 46/min.

vignette: A 63-year-old man with a heart attack two years ago has palpitations and feels light-headed. BP 92/60.
hints: Is the QRS narrow or broad?
Regular, broad, fast, and a scarred heart. Put it together.
explanation: A regular broad-complex tachycardia at about 175/min with identical QRS complexes. With a past MI, a broad-complex tachycardia is VT until proven otherwise. Clues to AV dissociation clinch it: P waves marching through at their own slower rate, and capture or fusion beats.
features: Broad QRS (about 165 ms), all the same shape
Dissociated P waves visible here and there
pearl: Assume any broad-complex tachycardia is VT until proven otherwise. After a previous MI, the vast majority are.

vignette: A 70-year-old woman with COPD has felt 'fluttery' and short of breath since yesterday.
hints: Ignore the QRS complexes. Look at the baseline between them.
A regular sawtooth at about 300/min.
explanation: Regular sawtooth flutter waves at about 300/min, with the AV node letting through every 2nd to 4th wave. The changing ratio makes the ventricular rhythm irregular, which can fool you into calling AF, but the atrial activity itself is perfectly regular and organised.
features: Sawtooth F waves at about 300/min (one per big square)
pearl: Flutter waves arrive once every big square (200 ms = 300/min). An organised, regular baseline means flutter, even when the QRS rhythm is irregular.

vignette: A 79-year-old woman has had two blackouts this week, one while sitting watching TV.
hints: Compare the PR before and after the dropped beat.
The PR never changes. A P wave just suddenly fails to conduct.
explanation: Regular P waves with a fixed PR interval, then a P wave suddenly fails to conduct (here 4:3). The broad QRS (bundle branch block) fits disease below the AV node. Mobitz II can progress to complete heart block without warning, which is why the blackouts matter.
features: Constant PR (about 180 ms) in conducted beats
Sudden non-conducted P wave; broad QRS
pearl: Mobitz I: PR stretches, then drops (usually the AV node, often benign). Mobitz II: PR fixed, then drops (usually below the node, high risk).

vignette: A 72-year-old woman with heart failure has a pre-op ECG before cataract surgery. No chest pain.
hints: Check the QRS width first. Then which way does V1 point?
Broad and deep in V1, broad notched R in V6, no small septal q waves.
explanation: QRS of 120 ms or more (here about 150), a deep broad QS in V1–V3, broad notched 'M-shaped' R waves in I, aVL, V5 and V6, and no septal q waves. The ST-T changes are discordant, pointing opposite to the QRS; that is expected in LBBB and is not ischaemia on its own.
features: Broad notched R in I, aVL, V5–V6; no septal q
pearl: WiLLiaM MaRRoW: W in V1 and M in V6 is LBBB; M in V1 and W in V6 is RBBB. LBBB hides ischaemia; the Sgarbossa criteria help in the right setting.

vignette: A 26-year-old man has had sharp chest pain for two days, worse lying flat and better leaning forward. He had a cold last week.
hints: Which coronary territory is the ST elevation in? All of them?
Look just before each QRS, and then at aVR.
explanation: Widespread concave ST elevation across several coronary territories (I, II, aVF, V2–V6), PR-segment depression, and the mirror image in aVR: ST depression with PR elevation. No reciprocal ST depression elsewhere. Sinus tachycardia is common, and pain that eases on leaning forward fits.
features: Diffuse concave ST elevation, not confined to one territory
aVR: ST depression with PR elevation
No reciprocal change except aVR and V1
pearl: PR elevation in aVR is the quiet tell of pericarditis. An ST/T ratio over 0.25 in V6 favours pericarditis over early repolarisation.

vignette: A 19-year-old woman felt her heart start pounding suddenly while bending to tie her shoelaces. She is otherwise well.
hints: Narrow or broad? Regular or irregular?
Regular, narrow, very fast, no visible P waves, sudden onset.
explanation: A regular narrow-complex tachycardia at about 185/min with no visible P waves (they are buried in or just after the QRS). Sudden onset and offset in a young, well person fits AV nodal re-entrant tachycardia, the commonest regular SVT, and one that is more common in women.
features: No P waves visible before the QRS
pearl: In AVNRT, look for a 'pseudo-r′' in V1 or 'pseudo-S' in the inferior leads: the retrograde P wave hiding at the end of the QRS.

vignette: A 48-year-old woman notices 'skipped beats' after her third coffee of the morning.
hints: Look at every second beat: early, broad, and no P wave in front.
Broad complex with a T wave pointing the opposite way, then a pause.
explanation: Every second beat is a premature, broad, bizarre QRS with no P wave before it and a T wave pointing the opposite way, followed by a full compensatory pause: ventricular bigeminy. In a structurally normal heart it is usually benign. Caffeine, alcohol, stress, low potassium or magnesium, and structural heart disease are the usual suspects.
features: PVC: early, broad (about 150 ms), no P wave
Discordant T wave and full compensatory pause
pearl: Full compensatory pause: the sinus beat after a PVC lands exactly two cycles after the one before it, because the sinus node never noticed the PVC.

vignette: An 82-year-old woman feels exhausted and dizzy. Pulse 38 and regular.
hints: Mark the P waves and march them out. Then do the same for the QRSs.
P waves and QRS complexes each keep their own regular rate and ignore each other.
explanation: P waves march through regularly at about 88/min, broad QRS complexes march at about 38/min, and the PR interval is random because nothing conducts. That is complete (third-degree) heart block with a ventricular escape rhythm. A narrow escape would suggest a higher, junctional escape, which is faster and more reliable.
features: Broad escape QRS regular at about 38/min
No consistent PR: complete AV dissociation
P waves hide in QRS and T waves
pearl: In complete heart block the atria beat faster than the ventricles. If the ventricles are faster, think of another cause of AV dissociation, such as VT.

vignette: A 69-year-old man on digoxin and a beta blocker feels tired. Pulse 48 and regular.
options: Atrial fibrillation with slow ventricular response
hints: Where is the P wave? Before the QRS, inside it, or after it?
Narrow QRS at 40–60/min with small inverted P waves just after it.
explanation: A regular narrow-complex rhythm at about 48/min with no P wave before the QRS; small inverted (retrograde) P waves sit just after it. The AV junction has taken over as pacemaker, at its intrinsic rate of 40–60/min, because the sinus node has slowed, here most likely from the drugs.
features: No P before the QRS; retrograde inverted P just after
pearl: Escape rates: sinus 60–100, junction 40–60, ventricle 20–40. Narrow at 40–60 is junctional; broad at 20–40 is ventricular.

vignette: A 58-year-old woman has a routine ECG for a new job. She is well, with no symptoms.
hints: Check the QRS width first. Then look at the shape in V1.
'Rabbit ears' rSR′ in V1, broad slurred S in I and V6.
explanation: QRS of 120 ms or more (here about 140) with an rSR′ 'M' in V1–V2, wide slurred S waves in I, aVL and V5–V6, and secondary T inversion in V1–V2. The right ventricle depolarises late, adding a terminal rightward wave. RBBB can be a normal finding, or reflect right heart strain (such as PE), ischaemia or congenital heart disease (such as an ASD).
features: Wide slurred S in I, aVL, V5–V6
pearl: Unlike LBBB, RBBB doesn't hide a STEMI: the start of the QRS is normal, so ST elevation stays readable.

vignette: A 54-year-old Aboriginal man presents to a remote clinic in the Northern Territory with an hour of crushing central chest pain.
hints: Which leads, and which artery supplies them?
Convex ST elevation V1–V4, lost R waves, and inferior reciprocal depression.
explanation: ST elevation from V1 to V5 (maximal in V2–V3) with hyperacute T waves and loss of R waves, plus ST elevation in I and aVL and reciprocal depression in III and aVF: an anterolateral STEMI from a proximal left anterior descending (LAD) occlusion. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people carry a higher burden of coronary disease and present younger, so chest pain at 54 gets taken seriously.
features: Loss of R waves in V2–V3
ST elevation in I and aVL
Reciprocal ST depression in III and aVF
pearl: ST elevation in aVL with inferior ST depression points to a proximal LAD occlusion, so a bigger territory is at risk.

vignette: A 66-year-old woman with diabetes has had two hours of upper abdominal discomfort and breathlessness. 'Just indigestion,' she says.
hints: The depression is horizontal and the T waves stay upright. Odd for ischaemia.
Mirror V1–V3 in your head: picture the back wall of the heart.
explanation: Horizontal ST depression in V1–V3 with upright T waves and a tall, broad R wave in V2 (R/S over 1). The anterior leads view the back of the heart from the front, so a posterior STEMI shows up upside down. Posterior leads V7–V9 would show ST elevation. It is a STEMI equivalent. Women and people with diabetes more often present without classic chest pain.
pearl: Flip the ECG over and hold it up to the light: the V1–V3 changes turn into Q waves and ST elevation.

vignette: A 57-year-old man collapses at a footy club barbecue. Bystanders start CPR; compressions pause while the AED analyses the rhythm.
hints: Can you find a single organised QRS complex?
Chaotic, irregular waves of changing size. No P, no QRS, no T.
explanation: Chaotic, irregular deflections of varying size and shape with no identifiable P waves, QRS complexes or T waves: ventricular fibrillation. It is a shockable cardiac arrest rhythm, which is exactly why early bystander CPR and a nearby AED save lives.
pearl: Coarse VF fades to fine VF, then asystole, over minutes. Survival drops by roughly 10% for every minute without CPR and defibrillation. Learn CPR.

vignette: A 17-year-old high-school runner has a sports ECG. The machine flagged 'irregular rhythm' and her mum is worried.
hints: Is there an identical P wave before every QRS?
The rate speeds up and slows down smoothly, in a cycle. Like breathing.
explanation: Every QRS has an identical upright P wave and a constant PR, but the rate drifts faster and slower in a smooth, repeating cycle. That is sinus arrhythmia: heart rate rises when breathing in and falls when breathing out. It is normal, especially in young, fit people.
features: Identical P waves before every QRS
R-R intervals vary smoothly and cyclically
pearl: Healthy hearts are not metronomes. Loss of sinus arrhythmia with age or diabetes reflects reduced vagal tone.

vignette: A 76-year-old woman admitted with a severe COPD flare is breathless on the ward. The monitor alarms for an irregular tachycardia.
hints: There ARE P waves. Do they all look the same?
At least three P-wave shapes, varying PR, irregular, over 100/min.
explanation: An irregular narrow-complex tachycardia at about 115/min with a P wave before every QRS, but the P waves come in at least three shapes and the PR interval keeps changing. That is multifocal atrial tachycardia, typically seen with severe lung disease, and it usually settles as the underlying illness does.
features: Three or more distinct P-wave shapes
pearl: The same picture under 100/min is called a wandering atrial pacemaker.

vignette: A 23-year-old woman has had episodes of sudden fast palpitations since her teens. This ECG is between episodes.
hints: Measure the PR interval. Short or long?
Look at the very start of the QRS: a slurred, ramp-like upstroke.
explanation: A short PR (under 120 ms), a slurred delta wave at the start of a broad QRS, and secondary ST-T changes: ventricular pre-excitation through an accessory pathway, the Wolff-Parkinson-White pattern. With symptomatic tachycardias it becomes WPW syndrome. A dominant R in V1 suggests a left-sided pathway, and negative delta waves in III can mimic inferior Q waves.
features: Dominant R in V1; pseudo-Q in III
pearl: AF in WPW looks like an irregular, very fast broad-complex tachycardia. It is dangerous because the accessory pathway has no 'speed limit' like the AV node.

vignette: A 19-year-old woman fainted the moment her alarm clock went off this morning. Her brother died suddenly and unexpectedly at 24.
hints: Measure from the start of the QRS to the end of the T wave.
The T wave ends well past halfway to the next QRS, and it's notched.
explanation: QTc about 590 ms (normal is under about 460 ms in women and 450 ms in men), with broad, notched T waves. Syncope triggered by a sudden noise plus a family history of sudden death fits congenital long QT syndrome, classically type 2 (notched T waves, startle or auditory triggers). It predisposes to torsades de pointes.
features: QT about 590 ms at 60/min (QTc about 590 ms)
T wave ends beyond the R-R midpoint
pearl: Triggers by type: LQT1 exercise and swimming, LQT2 sudden noise or emotion, LQT3 rest and sleep.

vignette: A 70-year-old woman is rescued after a fall on an overnight bushwalk in the Tasmanian highlands. Core temperature 30.5 °C; she is shivering.
hints: Note the fuzzy baseline and slow rate. Then look right after each QRS.
A dome-shaped hump at the J point, biggest in V3–V6.
explanation: Sinus bradycardia at about 42/min, a long QT, shivering artefact, and a positive hump at the J point (Osborn or J waves), most prominent in the mid and lateral chest leads. J waves grow as core temperature falls, and AF and ventricular arrhythmias become more likely as hypothermia deepens.
features: Osborn (J) waves at the end of the QRS
pearl: Osborn waves are not unique to cold: hypercalcaemia, brain injury and subarachnoid haemorrhage can produce them too.

vignette: An 84-year-old woman with a pacemaker attends her routine device check. She feels well.
hints: Look for very sharp, thin vertical lines.
Two spikes per beat: one before the P wave, one before a broad QRS.
explanation: Sharp pacing spikes come before both the P waves (atrial pacing) and the broad QRS complexes (ventricular pacing) at a steady 70/min: dual-chamber pacing. Pacing from the right ventricle gives a broad, LBBB-like QRS with discordant T waves, so it is neither LBBB nor VT.
features: Atrial spike, then a P wave
Ventricular spike, then a broad QRS
Regular at the programmed rate, about 70/min
pearl: Right ventricular apical pacing gives an LBBB-like QRS with a superior axis, so the QRS is negative in II, III and aVF.

vignette: A 38-year-old woman notices occasional 'thuds' in her chest when lying in bed at night.
hints: Find the early beats. Is their QRS narrow or broad?
Early narrow beats with an odd-looking P wave in front.
explanation: Sinus rhythm interrupted by early beats with a differently shaped (here inverted) P wave and a normal narrow QRS, followed by a pause that is not fully compensatory because the ectopic resets the sinus node. Premature atrial complexes are very common and usually harmless; caffeine, alcohol, stress and poor sleep are classic triggers.
features: Early beat with an abnormal P wave
Narrow QRS, same shape as the sinus beats
pearl: PVC: broad, no P wave, full compensatory pause. PAC: narrow, odd P wave, non-compensatory pause.

vignette: A 61-year-old man's heart has been 'just racing' since this morning. The monitor shows a rate stuck at 150.
hints: What's the exact rate? Is that a suspicious number?
Look between the QRS complexes for a second wave hiding in the T.
explanation: A regular narrow-complex tachycardia at almost exactly 150/min, with flutter waves at 300/min: one F wave shows between the QRS complexes and the next hides in the QRS and T wave. Atrial flutter with 2:1 block is easily mistaken for sinus tachycardia or SVT.
features: Every second F wave buried in the QRS or T
pearl: Any regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 150/min is flutter with 2:1 block until proven otherwise.

vignette: A 74-year-old woman reports brief light-headed spells. This strip catches one.
hints: During the gap, is there a P wave that failed to conduct?
No P wave at all, and the gap isn't a multiple of the normal P-P.
explanation: Normal sinus beats, then a gap of about 3 seconds with no P wave and no QRS, then sinus rhythm resumes. There is no non-conducted P wave, so this is not AV block: the sinus node itself paused. Recurrent symptomatic pauses point to sick sinus syndrome (sinus node dysfunction), common in older people.
features: No P wave during the pause
Pause not an exact multiple of the P-P interval
pearl: Pause an exact multiple of P-P: sinoatrial exit block. Not a multiple: sinus arrest. A P wave hiding in the preceding T: blocked PAC, the commonest cause of a pause.

vignette: A 60-year-old woman with long-standing high blood pressure has become breathless walking uphill.
hints: Measure: S wave in V1 plus R wave in V5.
Huge voltages, with asymmetric T inversion in the lateral leads.
explanation: Very tall R waves in V5–V6, I and aVL with deep S waves in V1–V2 (S in V1 + R in V5 about 47 mm; Sokolow-Lyon criterion is 35 mm or more), plus downsloping ST depression and asymmetric T inversion in the lateral leads (the 'strain' pattern) and mild discordant ST elevation in V1–V3. Long-standing hypertension is the usual cause; aortic stenosis and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy are others.
features: S V1 + R V5 about 47 mm (≥35 mm)
Lateral downsloping ST depression with asymmetric T inversion
pearl: Voltage criteria are insensitive, and young, slim people can exceed them without LVH. Strain changes make true LVH much more likely.

vignette: A 45-year-old woman has had three weeks of vomiting and diarrhoea and now has muscle cramps and weakness.
hints: What's that extra hump after each T wave?
Flat T waves, prominent U waves, mild ST depression.
explanation: Flattened T waves, prominent U waves (biggest in V2–V3, here taller than the T), mild ST depression and a long apparent QT that is really a QU interval: classic hypokalaemia. Vomiting and diarrhoea are common causes; diuretics are another. Low magnesium often comes along too.
features: Prominent U waves in V2–V3, taller than the T
pearl: In hypokalaemia, the T falls and the U rises. Mistaking the U for the T gives a falsely long QT.

vignette: A 49-year-old woman has had 30 minutes of crushing chest pain that started while shovelling soil. She is still in pain.
hints: No ST elevation. Look closely at where the ST segment starts in V2–V4.
Upsloping ST depression at the J point into tall, symmetrical T waves, plus ST elevation in aVR.
explanation: Upsloping ST depression of 1–3 mm at the J point in V2–V5, running into tall, symmetrical T waves, with slight ST elevation in aVR, in someone with ongoing chest pain. These de Winter T waves signal acute proximal LAD occlusion and are regarded as a STEMI equivalent, even with no ST elevation in the chest leads.
features: Upsloping ST depression at the J point, V2–V5
pearl: Tall T waves plus upsloping ST depression plus pain: think de Winter. Wellens, by contrast, appears once the pain has gone.

vignette: A 33-year-old woman, 20 weeks pregnant, has an ECG for occasional palpitations. This trace was recorded during one.
hints: Rate, rhythm, P waves, PR, QRS. Tick them off one by one.
Sometimes the answer is reassuringly boring.
explanation: Rate about 84/min, regular, an upright P wave before every QRS, PR about 160 ms, narrow QRS, normal ST-T: normal sinus rhythm. Resting heart rate rises by 10–20 beats/min in pregnancy and palpitations are common. A normal ECG captured during palpitations is reassuring.
features: Regular, with a P wave before every QRS
pearl: Read every ECG the same way: rate, rhythm, axis, intervals, morphology. A system beats a hunch.
